Org policy and security

For the person who installs Sigma across a team: what an organisation can lock, everything that can leave a machine, the two guards that sit outside the repository, what the threat model says, and how to report a vulnerability.

On this page
  • Organisation policy
  • What leaves the machine
  • The invocation adapter
  • The pre-push guard
  • The threat model in plain terms
  • Reporting a vulnerability

Most people only need

  • Sigma reports no usage data. Every outbound destination is opt-in, listed below.
  • Org policy is optional and needs something that writes .sdlc/managed-settings.json. Without it nothing changes.
  • The adapter pin and the pre-push patterns both live outside the repository, on purpose.
  • To report a vulnerability, use GitHub's private Report a vulnerability action.

This page is for people who set Sigma up for others. It adds to Trust and limits, which covers what Sigma refuses to do when it cannot be sure. Everything here is opt-in: a repository with none of these files behaves like the public default.

Organisation policy

An organisation can lock a few settings by putting a policy file at .sdlc/managed-settings.json. Sigma only reads it. The file is written by whatever manages the machine, such as a device-management tool or another policy writer; Sigma never writes it. A checkout declares it is adopted with managed_settings.project_id in .sdlc/config.json, or simply by having the file.

FieldMeaning
versionThe file format. Only 1 is read.
statusok, or access-revoked to lock a member out.
issued_at, refreshed_atTimes the policy was issued and last confirmed.
lockedThe values the organisation fixes. Only present when the status is ok.

Exactly three keys can be locked. A locked value overrides the local config.

Locked keyValueEffect
work.require_reviewa string such as changes or approvalWhich review a merge needs.
gates.hard_plan_gatea boolean, or an object with enabledWhether a plan is required before a pull request opens.
journal.enableda booleanWhether the event journal is on.

An unknown key inside locked is ignored. An unreadable or invalid file, an unknown version or status, or a revoked member makes the merge gate, the pull-request gate and the journal refuse. Everything else keeps working.

A deleted file does not switch policy off. The first time Sigma reads a valid file it records that the checkout is enrolled, in two places a one-file deletion does not reach, one of them inside the checkout's own git directory. If the file later disappears, the status reads enrolled-policy-missing and those gates refuse. Restore the file and the refusal clears by itself. If the checkout was deliberately removed from policy, the one local, network-free command that clears it is:

python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/managed_settings.py unenroll .sdlc
Detection, not a lock against the local user

Anyone who can write the checkout can delete the file and both markers, or run unenroll, and the checkout then reads as never enrolled. What this defends against is a one-file deletion, a stray cleanup, or a script that clears .sdlc/. Enrolment is learned at the first read after a valid file arrives, so a file delivered and deleted before any gate runs leaves no memory. A fresh clone that never held the file is not refused, because refusing it would be an outage.

What leaves the machine

Sigma reports no usage data. These are the only destinations, and each is opt-in.

DestinationWhat is sentWhenSwitch
GitHub, through ghthe issue, pull request and label traffic you ask forGitHub-backed backlogs, boards and pull requestsChoosing a GitHub backlog. The gh connection is outside Sigma's own recording.
Slack APIthe configured message payloadopt-in notificationSIGMA_SLACK_BOT_TOKEN
A configured webhookthe notification payloadopt-in channel notificationledger.autowatch.channel_webhook_url
An SMTP serverthe configured notificationopt-in agent-death notificationagent_watch.notify.email.enabled; an SMTP setting that comes from the repository also needs SIGMA_ALLOW_REPO_SMTP=1
Your agent host's model processthe prompt the host suppliesa model session you invokehost configuration
Model process for headless judge callsthe call's own prompt only; nothing from the project is loadedimport classifier, drift judge, unit assigner and validatorthe same gates as each caller
Model process for the drift judgethe question and reference document textshadow-mode judgment, off by defaultrulebook.drift.enabled plus a model name and a daily spend ceiling

The action log, timing store, phase transcripts and everything under .sdlc/ stay on the machine. Your agent host talks to its own model provider under that host's policy, which Sigma does not control. For a webhook, point it at a local adapter: one pointed at an Internet host is a listed high-risk case (see the threat model).

To check a command's destinations yourself, the repository has a capture tool that records destinations and whether a launch was intended, never request paths, bodies or field values. Its limits: it cannot see the inner connection of programs such as gh and git, only that they were launched, and Python started in isolated mode skips it.

The invocation adapter

Some hosts refuse the loop's own approval step as self-approval, and an environment marker cannot settle who is really approving, because the agent controls its own environment. So authority can be delegated to an adapter you install and pin outside the repository. It is off by default.

  • Where the pin lives. In your local git config for the checkout, never in a committed file. The repository's config.json can turn the adapter on but can never name the command or its hash.
  • What Sigma runs. Exactly the bytes you pinned, copied to a private file first, with no shell and a reduced environment. The file must be an executable you own, not group or world writable, and not a symlink.
  • Once, as the operator:
git config --local sigma.invocation.adapter.claude.path /absolute/path/to/adapter
git config --local sigma.invocation.adapter.claude.sha256 <sha256 of that file>
python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/invocation.py diagnose .sdlc claude

Use claude, codex or cursor as the id. diagnose prints installed-and-conforming, defer (no pin, the safe default) or refused. Then set "invocation": {"adapter": "claude"} in .sdlc/config.json.

What it is not

It is operator attestation, not isolation from the agent: a process running as you that can edit both your git config and the adapter file can pin an adapter of its own, so install and pin from a shell the agent does not control. It gates only Sigma's own approve-review verb; anything running as you can still post an approval comment with gh. No real Claude, Codex or Cursor adapter ships with Sigma, and host-visible relay is unproven on every host until an operator runs diagnose against a real one.

The pre-push guard

A small tool refuses a push whose new commits carry a denied pattern in a commit message or an added line. It scans only commits not already on any remote-tracking branch. A hit is reported as commit, surface and pattern line number, never the matched text. If any git command fails, it refuses rather than passing.

  • The patterns file holds one case-insensitive regular expression per line; blank lines and # lines are skipped. Keep it outside every repository: its contents are yours and are never committed. A pattern that does not compile, matches the empty string, or an empty file is refused by line number.
  • Install by creating .git/hooks/pre-push (mode 755) in the repository to protect:
#!/bin/sh
exec python3 /path/to/sigma/tools/prepush_scan.py --patterns /path/to/patterns.txt "$@"

Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 a hit (the push is refused), 2 a usage or patterns refusal (also refused). Fetch first: a stale remote-tracking branch widens the scan, never narrows it. It reads only git state, and git push --no-verify skips it, which is the operator's choice.

The threat model in plain terms

Sigma runs hooks and scripts on developer machines, reads and writes GitHub, and can start background workers. The threat model lists what it protects: your source and history, your GitHub state, credentials (the gh token, the Slack and SMTP secrets, the host's model credentials), the machine, and your model spend. It is an inventory, not a claim that every risk is gone.

Text from issues and comments is untrusted input. Repository content that reaches a command is untrusted too, so a shell command a repository supplies is refused by default; you grant it per checkout, after inspecting it, with git config --local sigma.allowRepositoryShellCommands true, which is local and never committed. The cases the model rates highest, as written there:

RiskResidualState
Prompt injection: an issue or comment asks a phase agent to run a command or edit labelshighno technical mitigation at that crossing; an open issue tracks it
A confident blocker match writes an edge to a third issuehighno technical mitigation; the reason weak wording is advisory only
A notification webhook aimed at an Internet host instead of a local adapterhighno technical mitigation; the webhook is opt-in
A Slack --unsafe-merge from the authorised channelmediumchannel membership is the only authority
A token-shaped value reaching a log or commentmediumknown patterns are scrubbed; coverage of every comment site is unverified
Managed policy deleted from an enrolled checkoutmediumthe checkout refuses; a writer who also removes the markers is not bound
A risky agent-host configuration (everything allowed, an unpinned package, a literal credential)mediumthe doctor reports it by file and rule, never a value; it does not block
A goal diff that deletes a hook, a CI step, the watcher or a ratchet baselinemediumflagged as a warning, not a block

Do not run an unattended loop on a repository you do not trust: it can carry its own .sdlc/config.json.

Reporting a vulnerability

Please report security vulnerabilities privately through GitHub's Report a vulnerability action on the repository's Security tab. This avoids exposing an exploitable issue in a public issue before maintainers can assess it.

The repository owner must enable GitHub private vulnerability reporting. If that channel is not available, contact admin@agrim.ai. Do not include secrets, access tokens or unredacted customer data in a report.

The stated aim is to acknowledge reports within 3 business days and to provide a fix or mitigation for a critical issue within 14 days. These are response targets, not a guarantee. Only the latest minor release is supported.
